2026-09-10.headline: Score HOLDS at 27/30 for a twenty-third consecutive edition — and it holds on one word in one rule. One. The oil channel now has its FIRST close. The scored Brent continuation closed $97.10 on 9 September, $2.10 ABOVE the $95 upgrade, its first close through the level since 24 July. What makes this different from July is not the level but the basis: on 23 and 24 July the continuation cleared $95 and the active contract did not, which is precisely why no upgrade fired (§9.36). On 9 September BOTH cleared — continuation $97.10, active $101.21 — the first such close since the channel was cut to 2 on 3 July, and the first on which both cleared, of any kind, since 3 June. §9.56 warned that a trigger level sitting INSIDE the basis has two defensible readings that give opposite answers; the level now sits below BOTH series — though the two readings still give opposite SCORING answers, one close against six, so §9.56 is narrowed rather than resolved. What holds the channel at 2 is the word sustained: the discipline that stopped three bad calls between 25 June and 15 July requires TWO confirmed closes, and there is one. A second close fires 2→3 and takes the score to 28. The 10 September mark is $97.00 and its session low is $96.96, both clear of the level — but a mark is not a close, and this document has been wrong exactly here. Two, and it is this document correcting itself. TWO CLAIMS PUBLISHED ON 9 SEPTEMBER ARE WITHDRAWN, AND BOTH ARE BAD DATES INSIDE A WINDOW. The kinetic count was published as no acknowledged US strike on Iranian soil from 1 September through the 8th. US forces struck Iranian radars ON 1 September and the President said so that day, so the window was wrong at its opening. Corrected: 2 through 9 September, eight days — the same count, a shifted window, and the 9th is now ON the record rather than uncounted. And Saudi Arabia did not strike Taiz and Marib in reply to the 8 September barrage: the source dates those strikes to the day BEFORE it. A Saudi reply was promised and is NOT SOURCED. Three. The curve’s war high has migrated DOWN it. The 2-, 5- and 10-year all closed at new war highs on 9 September; the 20- and 30-year did not, and have not since 17 August. The $39bn ten-year cleared 4.834% with primary dealers taking 4.31% of competitive-accepted, against 8.6% on 12 August. With the market priced near 56% for a HIKE on 16 September, this is the belly repricing POLICY, not the long end repricing fiscal risk — a different shock wearing the same yield. Four. The gas complex again set the records the oil complex did not: TTF €79.246 and Asia LNG ¥4,115, both war-record closes, while Henry Hub fell to a 7.87% discount to pre-war. bondYield.title: MARITIME DENIAL — 5/5, held. The adjudicating product is missing for a third edition, and this edition corrects the address it was being sought at.
bondYield.text: (i) The state. The downgrade requires a verified reopening AND traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions. (!) ‘NORMAL’ STILL HAS NO SINGLE DENOMINATOR — four baselines are in circulation this week at 85, 100, 130 and 138 vessels a day — so the test is run only where one provider supplies BOTH numerator and baseline (§9.19, §9.24). On Kpler’s own figures, 11 crossings on 8 September against a ~130/day pre-war base is under 9%. On JMIC’s, 39 facilitated transits per 48 hours against its own 138/day 2025 baseline is about 14% — and that numerator counts a US-facilitated SUBSET, not total traffic. No reading approaches 25% and no reopening has been verified by anyone. (ii) The trend inside one series. Kpler is the only provider with a clean week-on-week run, and it reads 5, 11, 6, 11 against its own 10-day mean of 13 — volatile, every reading below that mean, and the latest still 15% under it. Not recovering, and not flat either. (!) TankerMap, counting TANKERS ONLY, reads 1, 0, 0 across 8–10 September, which is a different universe and is reported beside the others rather than reconciled to them. (iii) What is new is not the count but the accumulation behind it: Windward records 38 vessels over 50 metres stationary at the northern Hormuz and Larak anchorage, most of them dark, building over several days. (!) A queue is not a transit statistic and is not treated as one, but it is the physical form the denial takes. (iv) A method correction that matters more than any number here: JMIC products are published on ukmto.org, and jmic.online is an unrelated academic journal. Three editions of failed retrieval were partly failures of address. 095 remains NOT OBTAINED, not absent.

bondYield.title: OIL PRICE SHOCK — 2/5, held on one word. The first of the two closes the rule requires has printed, $2.10 through the trigger, and both bases cleared it together for the first time since the channel was cut.
bondYield.text: (i) The scored continuation closed $97.10, +$2.72, $2.10 ABOVE the $95 upgrade level. The gap sequence that this document has tracked for a fortnight — $3.37, $2.68, $1.84, $0.62 — did not narrow again; it inverted. (ii) Why this is not July. The continuation also closed above $95 on 23 and 24 July, at $100.69 and $96.78, and no upgrade fired — because the ACTIVE contract closed $94.26 and $91.68 on those days, below the level, and §9.36 forbids reading a trigger across a roll. On 9 September the active closed $101.21. This is the first close since the channel was cut to 2 on 3 July on which both bases cleared $95, and the first close on which both cleared, of any kind, since 3 June. (!) §9.56 disclosed, before it went live, that a level sitting INSIDE the continuation-to-active basis has two defensible readings giving OPPOSITE answers, and warned the rule’s own text does not choose between them. That undefined region has closed in ONE sense only: the level now sits below BOTH series. (!) The two readings still give OPPOSITE scoring answers — the continuation has ONE close, the active has SIX — so §9.56 is not resolved, and the channel is held on the scored series exactly as before. The problem was flagged while the distance was still positive, exactly as §9.56c required, so nothing is being decided under the pressure of a fired trigger. (iii) What holds the channel at 2 is the word sustained, and nothing else. The discipline is two confirmed closes: it held oil at 3 on a sub-pre-war intraday on 2 July and cut to 2 only on the second close, and it held US-inflation at 3 on a 0.6 bp margin on 14 July and fired only on the second close. There is one close. (iv) The 10 September mark is $97.00, and its session low so far is $96.96 — the whole traded range of the morning sits above the trigger. (!) That is a mark, and §9.31 was written after an edition led on four intraday readings and withdrew all four by the next close. It is also true that the last two Singapore cuts UNDERSTATED the settle by $1.06 and $1.49, and that only 4 of the last 30 closes fell $2.10 or more, which is the distance from the 9 September CLOSE to the level. The channel is held on the rule, not on the arithmetic, and the arithmetic is not being hidden. (v) The downgrade is $24.62 away and irrelevant.

bondYield.title: US INFLATION IMPULSE — 5/5, held. A sixth close above the firing level, clearing by the widest margin of the run, with the breakeven at its highest since June.
bondYield.text: (i) The forward closed 2.3166%, a SIXTH consecutive close above the 2.30% level whose sustained break fired this channel 4→5 on 31 July. The six clear by 1.10, 0.96, 1.54, 0.82, 1.19 and 1.66 bp — 1.66 is the widest of the run. (!) The run itself is NOT monotone — the six margins oscillate — so the widening is one session old, not a trend. (ii) The documented downgrade is a sustained close at or below the 2.142% pre-war anchor, 17.46 bp lower, and it moved further away. (!) §9.16 and §9.26 govern the gap between the firing level and the downgrade level and the answer is unchanged: report the tension, do not close it. Converting a hysteresis rule into a symmetric trigger is the change that would have produced three wrong calls between 25 June and 15 July. (iii) The corroborating series says the same thing more plainly this time. Ten-year spot compensation closed 2.3879%, +1.28 bp, its highest since 3 June and 13.10 bp above its 2.2569% anchor. (!) One month ago this document was reporting BE10 at 0.21 bp above that anchor and asking whether a single basis point would put spot compensation below pre-war for the first time in the war. It has instead added 13 bp. The inflation-expectation complex has not merely failed to normalise; it has given back the entire mid-August normalisation — over the past MONTH, of which 1.28 bp came on 9 September. (!) No weekly breakeven figure is computed here, and the barrel’s weekly move on the scored series is +$5.01. (iv) The transmission is now legible in a way it has not been: the belly of the curve, where five-year real and breakeven pricing sits, produced the largest yield move on the board.

bondYield.title: TREASURY STRESS — 5/5, held. The war high has migrated DOWN the curve, and a ten-year cleared with almost no dealer backstop.
bondYield.text: (i) Both downgrade legs failed and both moved further away. The yield leg needs a 30-year close below 5.00% and the 30-year closed 5.2889%, failing by 28.89 bp, from 24.54. The volatility leg needs MOVE below 75 and MOVE closed 76.74, failing by 1.74, from 1.14 — a SECOND consecutive close on the wrong side after the sixth give-back of the war. (!) §9.15’s rotation does not apply: nothing rotated, both legs simply widened. (ii) The structural finding of this edition is where the records were set and where they were not. The 2-, 5- and 10-year ALL closed at new war highs — 4.4295%, 4.6163%, 4.8406% — while the 20- and 30-year did NOT, and have not exceeded their 17 August peaks of 5.3016% and 5.3060% in sixteen sessions. The moves were +3.59, +5.36, +5.24, +3.87 and +4.35 bp by tenor: the belly led and both wings lagged. (!) This is NOT a monotone shape and is not described as one; the 2s10s STEEPENED 1.44 bp on the day while the 5s30s flattened. (iii) Why it matters. For most of this war the long end led, which is the signature of a term-premium and fiscal-supply story. A belly-led selloff that leaves the 30-year 1.71 bp short of a three-week-old high is the signature of a POLICY story — and the market is priced near 56% for a 25 bp HIKE on 16 September, down from about 66% on 31 August, on a target range of 3.50–3.75%. A curve pricing a central bank into an oil shock is a different transmission from a curve pricing a fiscal risk premium, and it wears the same yield. (iv) The supply evidence points the same way. The $39bn ten-year reopening cleared 4.834% on 9 September against 4.683% on 12 August, with bid-to-cover 2.71 against 2.53 and indirects 79.18% of competitive-accepted against 76.7%. Primary dealers took 4.31%. On 12 August they took 8.6%. (!) The denominators are named because they differ: on total award ex-SOMA the same indirect figure is 78.98% (§9.40). (!) NO TAIL IS ASSERTED — Treasury publishes no when-issued level, so a tail is not computable from primary data (§9.39). The paper cleared 15.1 bp higher than the August auction that was itself reported as the highest ten-year stop since 2007, and it cleared it with the dealer backstop halved.

bondYield.title: POLITICAL STRESS — 5/5, held. The scored series printed a five-dollar handle for the first time since May, and its spread to the corroborating series set a war record.
bondYield.text: (i) AUTMUSAG resolved at $5.00 for 8 September, +7 cents, its first print at or above $5.00 since 28 May and 18 cents below its own $5.18 peak of 20 May. It is +42.0% on the $3.52 anchor, 25 cents above the $4.75 level that fired this channel 4→5 on 4 August, and 40 cents above the $4.60 downgrade condition — which needs THREE consecutive closes at or below it with no intervening print above $4.70, and is therefore not remotely live. The 9 and 10 September cells are blank. (ii) The §9.57 reconciliation moved this edition, and it moved against the series. Recomputed over the 36 dates since 5 January on which AUTMUSAG and the DOE regular series BOTH resolved, their spread means 64.7 cents and ranges 51.6 cents (16 February) to 77.3 cents (7 September) — a new maximum, and the NINTH consecutive weekly widening. (!) The 65.6-cent mean and 75.9-cent top carried since 4 September were computed over a window this document never stated, so the two are not comparable and neither is called wrong; the window and the count are stated here so that the next edition can test it. A structural spread that widens for nine straight observations is not stable, and the description of the scored series remains WITHDRAWN and unreplaced. (iii) The same-date gap to AAA is now measurable rather than merely asserted: AUTMUSAG $5.00 against AAA regular $4.1514 for 8 September, 84.9 cents apart, with AAA diesel at $5.9012 the same day. The scored series sits between the two AAA grades and matches neither. (iv) (!) And the record this channel could not see has resumed. AAA diesel set an all-time high of $5.9424 on 9 September, one session after the print this document reported as the end of the run. §9.61 stands: AUTMUSAG is a GASOLINE series measuring gasoline correctly, and whether a distillate belongs in this channel is a SCOPE question that is left open rather than settled here.

bondYield.title: ESCALATION RISK — 5/5, held. Two of this document’s own dates were wrong, the theatre widened to a fourth country, and the mediator has now been silent on the strait for four editions.
bondYield.text: (i) (!) THE KINETIC WINDOW PUBLISHED LAST EDITION WAS WRONG AT ITS START DATE AND IS WITHDRAWN. This document published ‘no acknowledged US strike on Iranian SOIL from 1 September through 8 September, an eighth day’. US forces struck Iranian radars on 1 September — the President said so on the record that day, and CENTCOM tied the strikes to IRGC attempts on shipping. The corrected window is 2 September through 9 September: the same eight days, shifted one, with the 9th now ON the record rather than uncounted because two independent conflict trackers report it clean. 10 September is unreported at the cut and is NOT counted. (!) The claim is bounded to SOIL and EXCLUDES strikes on vessels in Iranian waters — there were at least two near Kharg Island, on 5 and 8 September. (ii) (!) THE SECOND WITHDRAWAL IS ALSO A DATE. This document said Saudi Arabia struck Taiz and Marib ‘in reply’ to the 8 September barrage. The source dates the Saudi strikes on al-Jawf, al-Bayda, Marib and Taiz to the day BEFORE it. They did not answer the barrage; they preceded it. A Saudi response was promised in the words ‘all necessary measures’ and NO retaliatory target or date has been sourced. (iii) What genuinely widened. Iran fired 20 ballistic missiles at Al-Azraq air base in JORDAN overnight on 8–9 September — Jordan reports 18 intercepted, two down in open ground, no casualties. That is a fourth country taking fire. (!) On 9 September the IAEA Board also referred Iran to the UN Security Council, reported as the first such referral in twenty years; the vote count is NOT FOUND and none is asserted. Iran also attacked ten vessels near the strait and claims hits on two US destroyers (TIER 3 state media: uncorroborated). (iv) The exchange is now explicitly transactional: the Secretary of State said on 9 September that ‘for every time they try to hit US Navy ships, they’re going to lose tankers’. Eight Iranian vessels are claimed destroyed in two exchanges. (v) The mediator is missing for a FOURTH edition, and the negative is now checked at both ends. Oman published on 9 September — a call with the UN Secretary-General on ‘regional developments’ naming neither Hormuz, nor Iran, nor the IMO. The last Oman–Iran joint statement remains 25 August, and it does commit to a joint temporary corridor with phased mine-clearing — but it contains no mention of IMO registration. (!) The IMO end is checked directly this edition: its Hormuz page carries nothing after 13 April and no Iranian submission. Against that, the one live diplomatic thread is Qatari and Chinese, not Omani. (vi) And the President said on 9 September that talks ‘could happen’ but that the war would end ‘immediately’ after the November midterms — a timetable, offered by a principal, that runs to the 3 November midterms — 54 days, under eight weeks.

Both legs cleared by their widest margins of this arming: the 30-year by 8.89 bp, from 4.54, and the ten-year by 19.06 bp, from 13.82. The clearance sequence on the long leg reads 0.56, 4.23, 7.30, 5.71, 4.65, 4.23, 4.54, 8.89. (!) This document has said for a fortnight that 4.65% and 5.20% are the middle of the distribution rather than its edge, on the evidence of five in-and-out cycles each decided by under 6 bp. An eighth consecutive close, and a one-session jump to the widest margin of the arming, is the first evidence AGAINST that reading. (!) The sequence itself is NOT monotone, and it is recorded as such rather than absorbed into it

analysis.crossAsset: The full record, with every source dated and tiered, is at ANNEX A2.3. In brief. The EIA published its Short-Term Energy Outlook on 9 September and it is already behind the tape: it forecasts Brent near $90 for 2H2026 against a $97.10 scored close and a $101.21 active close the same day, because its own forecast was completed on 3 September, before the week’s rally, which was +$5.01 on the scored series. (!) Its supply numbers are the ones to keep: crude production shut-ins averaged 6.7 mb/d in August, up from 5.0 mb/d in July, with 5.7 mb/d forecast for Q4 — (!) so the same forecast has shut-ins EASING 1.0 mb/d from the August peak: the deterioration is realised, the improvement is forecast — and most flows not restored until Q2 2027. The Weekly Petroleum Status Report was delayed by Labor Day to 12:00 ET on 10 September and had NOT published at this cut, so §9.28’s import-reversion test — whether crude imports hold near 7.3 mb/d or revert to 6.3 — is unresolved for a SECOND cycle; the last print is 6.77 mb/d for the week ended 28 August. The September IEA report is due 11 September and the OPEC MOMR could not be retrieved at all. (!) The 0.07 mb/d effective OPEC spare-capacity figure has now failed re-verification twice and is RETIRED rather than carried: no primary source supports it this cycle, and the nearest available number is a third-party rendering of EIA data showing 0.00 mb/d for an observation month of May 2026, which is four months stale and not the same measurement (§9.19). Gas is the clearest attribution on the tape: QatarEnergy has extended force majeure on LNG cargoes into the autumn and EU storage is near 66% against a five-year seasonal norm around 80%, which is why TTF set a record while Henry Hub fell — US inventories run 5.2% above their five-year average on production near 112.9 Bcf/d. (!) TTF is quoted three ways this week — €79.246 on the scored series, €77.90 on a front-month continuous quote and a headline ‘above €80’ — and they are NOT averaged. On the calendar: August PPI at 08:30 ET on 10 September, CPI on Friday 11 September, and the FOMC on 15–16 September priced near 56% for a hike.

methodology.scale: Six channels, each scored 0–5 and summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch, 8–14 stress, 15–21 systemic-risk watch, 22–30 crisis. Maritime denial and escalation risk are EVENT channels and carry their own as-of dates; oil, US inflation, Treasury stress and political stress are MARKET channels and move only on confirmed closes. Five of six channels have been at the ceiling since 4 August, so the total cannot register further deterioration in five of the six dimensions it measures (§9.7). It equally cannot register improvement (§9.27). (!) This edition is the first in a long run where the caveat bites in ONE direction only. The scale is still hiding a great deal — a war that widened to Jordan, two gas records, three war-high yields — but the one channel with room is the one being tested: the oil channel sits one confirmed close from firing, and a move there would take the total to 28/30 on market data alone. Where the scale is saturated, read the composition and not the total.
methodology.scaleCap: (a) Confirmed closes only, and sustained means more than one. The oil channel held at 3 on 2 July through a sub-pre-war INTRADAY and was cut to 2 only on the second confirmed close, on 3 July. The US-inflation channel held at 3 on 14 July on a 0.6 bp margin because the trigger says sustained, and fired on 15 July on the second consecutive close. An oil downgrade taken on 25 June had to be reversed on the 26th. (!) That rule, and nothing else, is what holds this edition at 27/30. The scored continuation closed $97.10 on 9 September, $2.10 through the $95 upgrade level; that is ONE close. A second fires 2→3. (b) Hysteresis. Upgrades fire on a sustained break; downgrades require a sustained reversal past a WIDER threshold. This is why Treasury stress holds at 5 with MOVE below its trigger for two sessions in early August and why political stress held at 5 through a six-session gasoline decline that reversed completely on two backfills. (!) (c) The rule is never moved to fit the tape. The US-inflation downgrade sits 17.46 bp below the level whose break fired the channel, and that gap is reported rather than closed (§9.16, §9.26). The same discipline forbids re-basing the oil trigger onto whichever Brent series would fire it (§9.56b).
methodology.integrity: (!) An integrity rule written for a failure mode you have seen will not fire on one you have not, so each is stated by what it tests rather than by what it is for. §9.8 tests whether the PRIOR ROW failed to refresh at all — symptom, a zero gap on every field. It CLEARS this edition: eighteen fields moved on the 9 September row. §9.35 tests whether a single FIELD is identical to four decimal places to its predecessor, in which case it is UNRESOLVED and no day-on-day change may be asserted, regardless of whether the row around it is live. It CLEARS on the 8th, 9th and 10th — no such field on any of the three. The rule exists because on 17 August a 30-year identical to four decimals in an otherwise live row was published as genuine and concealed a new war high. (!) Its precision is per series: on a four-decimal yield an exact repeat is strong evidence of a carry, while on a two-decimal retail price it is close to a coin flip (§9.48). §9.41 tests every continuation against its active contract for a SIGN CHANGE or a STEP. It CLEARS: both bases widened smoothly. (!) A NEW STANDING CHECK IS ADDED THIS EDITION. A series that LOOKS derived must be tested against its own components before it is called derived: USYC2Y10 does NOT equal the ten-year less the two-year on any of the 179 rows in this extract, mean absolute difference 0.40 bp, so the ‘consistent by construction’ line this document carried for months is WITHDRAWN and the 2s10s counts as an independent observation. §9.60 tests, field by field, whether a cell the last edition PUBLISHED has since gone blank — the case both row-level rules assume cannot happen. It has FIRED for three consecutive extracts on the 7 September WTI, active-WTI and Henry Hub cells. A lost cell yields no close, so no d/d and no reconciliation entry, and the correct form of words is that the values existed and are gone, not that they were never there. §9.37 forbids computing a reconciliation gap against any field published as a carry, a restatement or a loss, because such a gap measures the extract rather than the timing of the cut. (!) It excluded the five-year this edition; that field settled 5.36 bp from its repeat, the second largest rate figure the table would have carried.

2026-09-11.headline: The score moves for the first time since 4 August. The oil channel fires 2→3 and the total goes to 28/30, ending a hold at 27 that ran twenty-three editions from 4 August. The rule asked for two confirmed closes above $95 and it has two: the scored Brent continuation closed $97.10 on 9 September and $102.72 on 10 September, and the 10 September session low of $96.14 never came back to the level. The active contract has seven such closes. §9.56 — the largest open methodological problem this document was carrying — is RESOLVED rather than narrowed: the trigger now sits below BOTH series, and 9 and 10 September are the only closes since the channel was cut to 2 on 3 July on which both bases cleared $95. Nothing was moved to make this fire: the $95 level is the one restated on 14 August, the series is the one the rule has always been written on, and the two-close reading of sustained is the one applied since 3 July. Two. The channel fired on the OTHER chokepoint. The move was not Hormuz. Houthi forces took the Red Sea port of Mokha on 10 September, putting Bab el-Mandeb — the outlet Saudi Arabia has been using around a denied Hormuz — under threat from the shore, and Riyadh told OPEC the same morning that its August crude output was 6.238 mb/d, the lowest since 1990, down 1.9 mb/d on the month. Brent rose $5.62 on the scored series — a big move and not a record, the eleventh largest of the war — and $6.42 on the active, which IS that series’ second-largest one-day rise of the war. Three. This document’s own reading of one session ago is SUPERSEDED and is named rather than dropped. The 10 September edition said the war high had migrated DOWN the curve, because the 20- and 30-year would not make new highs. On the 10 September close every tenor did, the 20- and 30-year taking out 17 August for the first time in sixteen trading sessions, and the two-year rose 15.61 bp — the largest one-day rise at that tenor in the whole war. Four. The auction points away from the long end. The $22bn 30-year reopening stopped THROUGH its when-issued by 2.7 bp at 5.308%, with primary dealers taking 2.21%, the lowest on record. The selloff was the 08:30 PPI — +5.4% year on year, the highest of 2026, diesel +24.1% on the month — not indigestion. August CPI is PROSPECTIVE at this cut. Five. CENTCOM’s five-tanker claim is CORROBORATED: JMIC 095 was obtained after three editions of failure and carries all five by name and UKMTO reference. Sequencing 27 → 27 → 27 → 27 → 28.

bondYield.title: MARITIME DENIAL — 5/5, held. The adjudicating product arrived after three editions of failure, and it unfroze a count that had not moved since 5 September.
bondYield.text: (i) The state. The downgrade requires a verified reopening AND traffic above 25% of normal for ten sessions. Neither leg has a candidate. Run where one provider supplies BOTH numerator and baseline (§9.19, §9.24): Kpler’s 10-day mean of 10 vessels a day at 9 September, against its own pre-war base above 130, is under 8% — and Kpler itself calls it the lowest since May. (ii) JMIC 095 is the substance of this edition on this channel. The incident count moves 101 → 109 since 1 March, so the count Update 094 froze at 101 is unfrozen — a freeze reported in each of the two editions that followed 094, across three of which 095 could not be retrieved. (!) Its internal arithmetic does not reconcile — ‘7 incidents since the last report’ added to 094’s 101 gives 108 — and the discipline here is to publish both figures verbatim, adjust neither, and let the next product settle it. (iii) The mine language moved and the direction is not reassuring. 094 asked mariners to watch for ‘mining activity in the area’. 095 asks them to watch for ‘attempted mining activity within and adjacent to the TSS’. That is narrower in geography and different in tense; it is not a statement that the mines are gone, and it is the fourth allied product since the presidential mine-free claim of 25 August that declines to say so. (iv) (!) The channel acquired a SECOND theatre this window and the score cannot show it, which is the scale-cap problem in its purest form: Bab el-Mandeb and the Gulf of Aden are carried at SUBSTANTIAL in the same product that carries Hormuz at SEVERE, and on 10 September Houthi forces took the Red Sea port that overlooks the first of them. (!) That SUBSTANTIAL rating PREDATES the seizure and is NOT evidence about it; the two facts sit side by side and are not combined.

bondYield.title: OIL PRICE SHOCK — 2/5 to 3/5. FIRES. The second confirmed close printed $7.72 through the trigger, the discipline that delayed it by one edition cost nothing, and the move came from the OTHER chokepoint.
bondYield.text: (i) The rule is satisfied on its own terms. The scored continuation closed $97.10 on 9 September and $102.72 on 10 September, +$5.62: two consecutive confirmed closes above $95, which is what ‘sustained’ has meant in this document since 3 July. The second close cleared by $7.72 and the session low of $96.14 never came back to the level. Nothing was moved to make this fire — not the level, not the word, not the series (§9.26). (ii) §9.56 is RESOLVED, and the resolution is the strongest possible one. The problem was that a trigger sitting INSIDE the continuation-to-active basis had two defensible readings giving OPPOSITE answers. On 9 September the level sat below both series but the readings still disagreed on the SCORE, one close against six. On 10 September the active closed $107.63, a seventh straight close through the level, and the continuation took its second: both readings now fire. The undefined region is gone in both senses, and it closed without the rule ever being rewritten under pressure. (iii) The one-edition delay is the vindication, not the cost. On 10 September this document had ONE confirmed close and a mark of $97.00 whose low so far was already through the trigger. Two shortcuts were available and BOTH were refused: counting the mark as the second close, and shortening sustained to a single close. Either would have fired the channel a session early on reasoning that happened to be right — which is exactly how 25 June produced a downgrade reversed the next day. (!) And the mark understated twice over: the close came in $5.72 above it, and the settled session low of $96.14 was 82 cents below the low the morning had shown. (iv) Why the barrel moved ON 10 SEPTEMBER, and it was NOT Hormuz. (!) This attributes the SECOND close only; the 9 September close is not attributed here, and carried the previous window’s events. Two dated items land inside the 10 September session, and neither is a Strait event. Houthi forces seized Mokha, on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, putting Bab el-Mandeb at risk — which a bank’s framing relayed this week calls the remaining seaborne exit Saudi crude has used AROUND a denied Hormuz. And Saudi Arabia reported to OPEC that August output was 6.238 mb/d, the lowest since 1990, down about 1.9 mb/d on the month. (!) The producer’s own submission, but it reaches this desk through a TIER 2 relay; the submission itself is not published. (!) The price is therefore pricing a SECOND chokepoint against a producer already at a 36-year low, and this document’s own maritime channel — scoped to Hormuz — cannot register either. (v) The reconciliation is the most one-directional of the war. FIFTEEN marks were published for 10 September; FOURTEEN settled ABOVE them and only the 2s10s below. Brent missed by +$5.72, after +$1.06 and +$1.49 — a THIRD consecutive upside miss, and by far the largest. The Singapore cut is systematically understating a rising tape and that is now a documented pattern, not an anecdote (§9.31). (vi) (!) WHAT THIS EDITION DOES NOT DO IS SET THE NEW LEVELS. The 3→4 upgrade is NOT on this document’s current record — the channel has sat at 2 since 3 July and the trigger table has only ever restated the live level — and no 3→2 downgrade is set here either, because §4(b) requires a downgrade threshold WIDER than the upgrade that just fired, so it cannot be the mirror of $95. Setting either level on the day a trigger fires is precisely what §9.26 forbids. Both are OPEN, flagged, and are the first thing the next edition must publish — before the price is near them.

bondYield.title: US INFLATION IMPULSE — 5/5, held. A seventh close above the firing level at the widest margin of the run, and the producer data finally shows the barrel arriving.
bondYield.text: (i) The forward closed 2.3295%, a SEVENTH consecutive close above the 2.30% level whose sustained break fired this channel 4→5 on 31 July, clearing by 2.95 bp — the widest of the run, nearly double the previous widest, and the highest close since 20 August. (!) The margins still oscillate rather than trend, and are recorded as such. (ii) The documented downgrade is a sustained close at or below the 2.142% anchor, 18.75 bp lower, from 17.46: further away again. (!) §9.16 and §9.26 govern the gap between firing level and downgrade level; the answer is unchanged and the tension is reported rather than closed. (iii) The transmission is no longer an inference. August producer prices, published 08:30 ET on 10 September, rose 0.4% on the month and 5.4% on the year — the highest annual rate of 2026 — with final-demand energy +4.2% accounting for more than three-quarters of the goods increase and diesel alone +24.1%. That is the oil channel appearing in the price statistics, one month before it can appear in the retail series this document scores for political stress. (iv) Ten-year spot compensation closed 2.4165%, +2.86 bp, its highest since 21 May and 15.96 bp above its 2.2569% anchor. It carried 2.86 of the ten-year’s 12.20 bp: compensation, not real yield, but under a quarter of the move, so the ten-year sold off mostly on real rates. (v) (!) August CPI is PROSPECTIVE at this cut, at 08:30 ET today, and is the last inflation reading before the FOMC. Consensus is +0.4% headline and 3.4% on the year, with core 2.4% on the year. (!) The core MONTHLY consensus is quoted at +0.4% by one dated source and +0.2% by another; the two are NOT averaged and both are named.

bondYield.title: TREASURY STRESS — 5/5, held. Every tenor made a war high, the two-year by the largest one-day move of the war, and the auction says the long end is not the problem.
bondYield.text: (i) Both downgrade legs failed and both widened sharply. The yield leg needs a 30-year close below 5.00%; it closed 5.3652%, failing by 36.52 bp, from 28.89. The volatility leg needs MOVE below 75; MOVE closed 82.09, failing by 7.09, from 1.74 — the miss quadrupled in one session on a THIRD consecutive close on the wrong side. (ii) (!) THE LAST EDITION’S STRUCTURAL READING IS SUPERSEDED AFTER ONE SESSION AND IS NAMED HERE RATHER THAN DROPPED. It said the war high had migrated DOWN the curve, because the 2-, 5- and 10-year made new highs while the 20- and 30-year would not. On the 10 September close all five made new highs, the 20-year at 5.3915% and the 30-year at 5.3652%, taking out the 17 August peaks after sixteen trading sessions — seventeen rows, one of them the shut Labor Day market (§9.58). The reading was correct on the data it had and survived one session. (iii) The SHAPE, however, says the same thing the migration reading was trying to say. The moves fall monotonically with tenor — +15.61, +14.55, +12.20, +10.07, +7.63 bp — a clean bear flattener, 2s10s −3.195. The two-year’s 15.61 bp is the largest one-day rise at that tenor in this entire war, past the 13.27 of 17 June. A front-led selloff prices a CENTRAL BANK. (iv) And the auction points away from the alternative. The $22bn 30-year reopening stopped at 5.308% against a 5.335% when-issued — a 2.7 bp stop THROUGH, not a tail — on a bid-to-cover of 2.612 against a recent 2.38 average, indirects 79.5% and primary dealers 2.21%, the lowest on record, against 11.51% at the 13 August new issue. (!) The when-issued level is a dealer-desk figure, TIER 2, not Treasury primary data, so the stop-through is reported at that tier and §9.39 is not relaxed. It is the highest 30-year stop since August 2001 and the fifth consecutive above 5%; it is a REOPENING and is not comparable with the $25bn new issue that cleared 5.216%. A long end absorbed at a record-low dealer take is not a buyer strike. (v) (!) WITHDRAWN: the hike-odds comparison published last edition. This document wrote that the market was priced near 56% for a hike, ‘down from about 66% on 31 August’. The two figures are from different venues: the 66% is CME FedWatch, the 56% a prediction-market price, and differencing across them is what §9.19 forbids. The comparison is withdrawn; the DIRECTION it implied is not asserted to have been wrong. On one venue CME reads 44% a month before 9 September, 66% on 31 August, 62% on 9 September, and higher again after the PPI — up over the month, modestly down across the fortnight the withdrawn sentence spanned. From here the venues are published separately and never differenced: CME 62% (9 Sep), prediction market 54% (11 Sep).

bondYield.title: POLITICAL STRESS — 5/5, held. The scored series matched a four-month high, and the record it cannot see was set twice more.
bondYield.text: (i) AUTMUSAG resolved at $5.05 for 9 September, +5 cents. (!) It is the highest since 27 May, when it last printed exactly $5.05 — so it MATCHES that level rather than exceeding it, and the distinction is made because this document has mislabelled a match as a record before. It sits 13 cents below the $5.18 peak of 20 May, +43.5% on the $3.52 anchor, 30 cents above the $4.75 level that fired this channel 4→5 on 4 August, and 45 cents above the $4.60 downgrade condition, which needs THREE consecutive closes at or below it. The 10 and 11 September cells are blank. (ii) §9.57’s spread is UNTESTED this edition, not stable. The DOE series is WEEKLY and next prints on 14 September, so the record 77.3-cent spread of 7 September and its ninth consecutive widening are neither extended nor reversed. The description of the scored series remains WITHDRAWN and unreplaced. (iii) The same-date gap to AAA regular NARROWED for the first time in this run, to 82.6 cents — AUTMUSAG $5.05 against AAA regular $4.2245 for 9 September — from 84.9 cents on the 8th. One session is not a turn. (iv) (!) The distillate record ran again, twice. AAA diesel set an all-time high of $5.9424 on 9 September and another at $5.9773 on 10 September, +3.49 cents, and sits 2.27 cents below $6.00. On the same day GasBuddy’s separate national average crossed $6.00 for the first time on record. (!) The two series are different panels and are NOT spliced; a six-dollar headline is true of one national series and not yet of the other, and both statements are published. §9.61 stands: AUTMUSAG is a GASOLINE series measuring gasoline correctly, and whether a distillate belongs in this channel is a SCOPE question left open rather than settled here — but the producer data above now puts +24.1% of monthly diesel inflation directly into the channel this document scores on gasoline.

bondYield.title: ESCALATION RISK — 5/5, held. A second chokepoint changed hands, the Saudi reply this document could not source has been sourced, and the file acquired its first hard dates.
bondYield.text: (i) The war acquired a SECOND theatre of maritime denial. Houthi forces took the Red Sea port of Mokha on 10 September, government forces withdrawing south — Reuters citing three Yemeni government sources, with a correspondent on the ground. Bab el-Mandeb is about 29 km at its narrowest, and the defence analyst quoted says the strait could be controlled ‘just with artillery’, without missiles or drones. Yemen’s presidential council head said it ‘cannot become another Strait of Hormuz’. (!) Against that, the Houthi spokesman says navigation and trade ‘remain safe and uninterrupted’ — while the ban on Saudi ships stands, and both halves are recorded. (ii) (!) THE SAUDI REPLY IS NOW SOURCED, which discharges an open item published last edition as promised-and-NOT-SOURCED. Saudi forces struck Taiz, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib on 10 September: 40 strikes on one count, 54 on the Houthis’ own. TWO counts, named to their sources and never merged. (iii) The 8 September barrage that prompted it is now on the UN record in Saudi Arabia’s own words — its ambassador condemned ‘the September 8 strikes that wounded 73 civilians’ on 10 September — which independently confirms the date correction this document published yesterday. (iv) The kinetic window extends to 2 through 10 September, NINE days with no acknowledged US strike on Iranian SOIL; 11 September is unreported at the cut and is NOT counted. (!) One counter-indication is named rather than buried: Iranian state media reported projectiles striking areas of Sirik, timestamped late 9 / early 10 September, with damage and casualties explicitly not available. It is TIER 3, unacknowledged by CENTCOM, and does not meet the bar of ‘acknowledged’ — but it is the second such claim at Sirik after 1 September and the window is published with it on the record. (v) Mediation was replaced by a calendar. A FIFTH consecutive edition with no Omani text on the strait (§9.23). What exists instead is dated: the IAEA Board referred Iran to the Security Council on 9 September by 23 to 3 with 8 abstentions, the three being Russia, China and Niger; the Council met on 10 September with its Iran sanctions committee blocked a fourth consecutive quarter; and the expert panel’s mandate comes to a vote on 17 September and expires 27 September. That is the first hard deadline on this file all war. (vi) (!) One damage claim is deliberately NOT adopted. A single source reports an A-10 wing and about eight F-15E aircraft damaged at Muwaffaq Salti by the Al-Azraq salvo. It contradicts Jordan’s own TIER 1 statement that the two leakers fell in unpopulated areas. Both are on the record and neither is adopted here.

NOT ARMED — and for the first time NOT ARMED ON EVIDENCE rather than on untestability. The sequence is still not monotone and is recorded as such

NOT ARMED. 82.09, some 47.91 points below, and the war high of 115.02 was set on 26 March. (!) The direction is what carries: MOVE has risen 5.35 points in a session, closed above its 73.38 pre-war anchor for a THIRD session, and is at its highest since 31 July, while the 30-year sits 75.46 bp above its own anchor. analysis.crossAsset: The full record, with every source dated and tiered, is at ANNEX A2.3. (!) §9.28’S IMPORT TEST IS RESOLVED AFTER TWO UNRESOLVED CYCLES, AND IT RESOLVES TO NO REVERSION. The September IEA report was due at 10:00 Paris on 11 September and is PROSPECTIVE. Gas remains the clearest attribution: TTF €82.047 and Asia LNG ¥4,198 set records while Henry Hub closed 7.48% BELOW pre-war — a routing and loading shock, not a global one. On freight, the Baltic TD3C was last assessed at WS677.22 with a round-trip TCE near $704,000/day for 3 September; (!) the current week is NOT FOUND and the figure is published with its date, not as a current level. War-risk cover for a Gulf transit is quoted at 7.5–12.5% of hull value against about 0.25% pre-conflict, dated 8 September — (!) a percentage-of-hull basis NOT combined with the per-voyage dollar figures also in circulation. methodology.scale: Six channels, each scored 0–5 and summed to 0–30. Bands: 0–7 watch, 8–14 stress, 15–21 systemic-risk watch, 22–30 crisis. Maritime denial and escalation risk are EVENT channels and carry their own as-of dates; oil, US inflation, Treasury stress and political stress are MARKET channels and move only on confirmed closes. Five of six channels have been at the ceiling since 4 August. (!) This edition is where the standing caveat earns its keep. Since 10 July this document has said that further geopolitical deterioration CANNOT raise the score, because maritime and escalation are capped, and that only a MARKET channel could move the number. On 10 September the war widened to a second chokepoint — and the score moved, through the barrel, by one point. The move is not a measure of the escalation; it is a measure of the instrument. What the total still cannot show: the fall of Mokha, a seventeenth TTF record, a fourteenth Asia LNG record, five war-high Treasury closes, a 30-year absorbed at a record-low dealer take, and a diesel record set twice in two days. (!) 28/30 leaves two points of headroom and both sit in the oil channel, which is now the only channel below its cap.
methodology.scaleCap: (a) Confirmed closes only, and sustained means more than one. The oil channel held at 3 on 2 July through a sub-pre-war INTRADAY and was cut to 2 only on the second confirmed close, on 3 July; the US-inflation channel held at 3 on 14 July on a 0.6 bp margin and fired on the 15th on the second close; an oil downgrade taken on 25 June had to be reversed on the 26th. (!) The 10 September edition applied that rule at its most uncomfortable: it held the oil channel at 2 on a mark of $97.00 whose session low was ALREADY through the trigger, and said in terms that a mark is not a close. The close came in $5.72 above the mark. The delay cost one edition and bought the certainty that the upgrade rests on two settled prices rather than on a morning quotation that happened to be right. (b) Hysteresis. Upgrades fire on a sustained break; downgrades require a sustained reversal past a WIDER threshold. (!) That rule now binds this document in a new place. Having fired oil 2→3 on $95, a symmetric 3→2 downgrade at $95 is FORBIDDEN by (b), and no wider level is on the record. No level is set in this edition, because §9.26 forbids setting one under the pressure of a trigger that has just fired — the same reasoning that refused to move the 5y5y firing level in August. The 3→4 upgrade is likewise not on the record and is not invented. Both are OPEN, and the next edition must publish both, before the price is near either.
methodology.integrity: §9.19 forbids splicing two series that measure different things, however similar their labels. It is applied five ways in this edition. The FIVE retail fuel series are kept apart, which is why a six-dollar diesel headline is reported as true of GasBuddy’s national panel and not yet of AAA’s. The five transit universes are kept apart, and the maritime percentage-of-normal test is run only where one provider supplies both numerator and baseline. War-risk cover quoted as a percentage of hull value is not combined with figures quoted in dollars per voyage. The SPR figure for 28 August is not carried forward as a current level. (!) And the rule caught a failure of this document’s own: the 10 September edition reported the September hike as ‘near 56%, down from about 66% on 31 August’, splicing a prediction-market price onto a CME FedWatch series. That comparison is WITHDRAWN. The error was not merely one of precision — it inverted a direction, reporting a market backing away from a hike when the CME series had risen from 44% to 62% over the month. The two venues are now published separately and never differenced across. §9.23 governs negatives: a negative claim is a claim about a SOURCE, and must be probed a second, different way. The CENTCOM negative rests on the press-release index read directly plus DVIDS as an independent host; the pagination parameter is known to be ignored on that index and is NOT counted (§9.64). The JMIC 096 negative is stated as NOT YET PUBLISHED on a 404 against a constructed URL, and no claim is made that it does not exist. (!) §9.65: a date, a window and a source ADDRESS are all figures, and are withdrawn by name when wrong. Last edition withdrew two dates; this edition withdraws a spliced probability and supersedes a structural reading of its own that was one session old.

methodology.intraday: §9.56 was opened on 2 September and has been described since as the largest open methodological problem in this document. The problem: the $95 oil trigger is written on the CONTINUATION series (CO2), but the continuation and the ACTIVE contract (COA) diverged after the 31 August roll, and the trigger level sat BETWEEN them. Two defensible readings — score the series the rule names, or score the contract the market trades — gave OPPOSITE answers, and the rule’s own text did not choose. §9.56c required the problem to be disclosed while the distance was still positive, so that nothing would be decided under the pressure of a fired trigger, and it was. The resolution came in two steps and neither involved changing the rule. On 9 September the level fell below BOTH series — CO2 $97.10, COA $101.21 — which removed the geometric ambiguity but not the scoring one, because the continuation had one close and the active had six. On 10 September the continuation took its second close, at $102.72, while the active took a seventh at $107.63. Both readings now fire, so §9.56 is RESOLVED and CLOSED. (!) Two things are recorded so the resolution is not over-claimed. First, the rule remains written on the continuation, and if the two series diverge across a future roll the ambiguity returns; §9.36 and §9.36b are unchanged and both bases are still quoted wherever a trigger distance appears. Second, the resolution was luck as much as design — the price moved far enough fast enough that the readings converged.
